references.text: The context for the parable of the dishonest manager, where the manager is called in to give an account. The manager's strategy of reducing the debt notes begins in [ref:Luk 16:1|Luke 16:1].

The next step in the manager's plan: after reducing the first debtor's debt from one hundred baths of oil to fifty, he asks the next debtor what he owes and also reduces his debt ([ref:Luk 16:7|Luke 16:7]).

A "bat" (βάτος) was a Hebrew unit of measure for liquid goods. In [ref:1 Kong 5:11|1 Kings 5:11], the bat is mentioned as a unit of measurement, providing background for the quantities mentioned in the parable.
The bath as a unit of measure is mentioned in [ref:Esek 45:14|Ezekiel 45:14], where it is explained that a bath is one-tenth of a homer. One hundred baths of oil was therefore a significant amount.
The Lord praises the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. The manager's action of reducing the debt notes—as in verse 6—is paradoxically commended ([ref:Luk 16:8|Luke 16:8]).
Jesus' teaching on using unrighteous mammon to make friends. The manager's action in verse 6 illustrates exactly this strategy ([ref:Luk 16:9|Luke 16:9]).

In [ref:Jes 10:1-2|Isaiah 10:1–2], there is a warning against those who write unjust laws and record injustice. The manager's manipulation of the debt notes (γράμματα) in Luke 16:6 can be seen in light of this motif of document forgery.
